utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before having the next witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to raise? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just very briefly, and as I have informed Defence counsel, though I wasn't of course able to speak in B/C/S to Mr. Stojanovic, that as we have continued to learn about the law of genocide, I think we learned a little more a few hours ago. And it appears that our complicity in genocide charge, while it incorporates some of the facts we have involved here, it appears that from the ruling that aiding and abetting in genocide may be the more specific and better charge now based on the most recent opinion. We're of course studying that. But given that, it appears as though we will be needing to file an amended indictment to include aiding and abetting in genocide. Aiding and abetting is of course charged but it is not charged specifically to genocide, I don't believe, from the old indictment. I just wanted to put everyone officially on notice of that, and we're just trying to keep up with the current law on this matter, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, I guess. The rules are getting changed as the game is being played. I don't know how it's going to impact our case. I need to see it. It's kind of interesting. I just heard part of the decision, how they got to aiding and abetting in genocide, something that doesn't exist, at least I'm unaware of, and the reasoning behind it. So we probably will be objecting for a variety of reasons, one of that fact that we're well into our case. And number two, I believe at least, you know, from what I've heard, and I have to give it some more thought, that perhaps the Appeals Chamber exceeded its mandate under the -- in creating the Tribunal, because now it appears that they are creating law, something which they're not supposed to be doing. But in any event we're going to have to wait and see. And I assume that if they're going to be amending the indictment, they're going to be throwing out the complicity in genocide portion, unless what I'm hearing is they also want to charge in the alternative to this new addition of aiding and abetting. And of course I'd have to wait and see, and I don't know how that will impact my case because I may need some additional time as a result of this amended indictment. I'm just putting everybody on notice as well. Because I think it's rather unfair to charge Mr. Blagojevic back in 1999 on something, then investigate the case, we start the trial, we have all these amendments, and now in the middle of the game we're amending the indictment yet again. So -- but I can understand why they want to do it, but nonetheless I think there's some fundamental unfairness about all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I think this morning I just listened to the delivery of the summaries of the judgement. I haven't read the whole text of the judgement. And that before that, I think I should refrain from making any comments at this moment. But we would like to thank the Prosecution for informing us about their intention. I also hope the Prosecution could have a thorough reading of that judgement before jumping. And another matter is that as we said before that we were not quite satisfied with the 65 ter filings submitted by the Defence, and during the examinations of the first witness we found something new in his testimony about the whereabouts of Mr. Blagojevic, which did not appear in the 65 ter filings. So in this case, I believe that the Defence should submit to the other party and to the Trial Chamber proofing notes indicating that important element, which may be exculpatory to your client, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. That was something that we did learn. And I did inform the Prosecution of new developments with these witnesses, but I will -- if I'm being ordered by the Court to provide proofing notes, I will do so, recognising that, at least for technical purposes, it's not in the rules. Nonetheless, I accept that. I only mention that so in the event I want for us to go outside the rules, outside the box, in some of my requests, that I'm not held strictly to the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, our interpretation is that the proofing notes are supplementary to the 65 ter filings. The witness came here and you have a proofing session with the witness. Suddenly the witness mentioned something that is not listed in your 65 ter filings. So by doing so, we could avoid the wasting of time and any pre-emptive attacks on the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You just have to list that new information or elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If there's no new information, I don't think there's a need to submit proofing notes on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Since we're on that topic, this witness did inform us something new last night. I already spoke to the Prosecutor about it. It was about a meeting that he attended on July 12th at the SDS headquarters, where Mr. Deronjic was there. The phone rang; it was President Karadzic who congratulated -- then the phone was put on speakerphone to everybody could hear the president congratulating everybody on the liberation of Srebrenica. Then the witness said he heard Karadzic directly speak to Deronjic saying words to the effect that: You are -- everything is under your control, or words to that effect. So that's the only new development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your information. I hope for the next witness you could submit something in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And are there any protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Blagojevic wishes to say something; however, in light of the situation, I prefer that it be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We are going into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Witness, do you mind if I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I saw you come into the room with a notebook in your hands. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the law on defence and law on the army, published in June of 1992, pursuant to which I as chief of the department of the Ministry of Defence had to work and abide by the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any objections from the Prosecution on that copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I be heard for one second, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have made a copy of that law from the Official Gazette. That will be introduced as D60 -- it's already introduced. I beg your pardon. It has already been introduced, but this is his personal copy. We have notified the Prosecutor that we would be using this, and the gentleman came to The Hague with his own copy. We can provide him with a fresh copy as we go through this. We're just going to briefly make reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess there's no objections from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We may want to take a look at the original, but at this point there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I ask this question just to spell out any suspicions on that issue. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I was going to do that first thing myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name and give us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Aleksandar Tesic. A-l-e-k-s-a-n-d-a-r T-e-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So your last name is T-e-s-i-c. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Tesic, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Today I live in Ljubovija, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I work at the Ministry of Defence, Bratunac department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How long have you worked there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Since the 1st of March, 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before we speak about your work, could you please tell us where you grew up.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 23rd of January, 1954, in Bratunac, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I grew up there, completed elementary school there. I attended secondary school and completed secondary school in Ljubovija, in Serbia. Following that, I attended physical education college in Belgrade. I studied there for three years as a full time student and unfortunately did not complete the college. I hadn't studied enough. I lived in Bratunac up until 1988, at which time I bought a plot of land in Ljubovija and built a house there. I moved into the house in 1990. As I am a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was in the -- I was recorded in the military books in Bratunac and I was recorded in those books back in 1971. And my name has remained in the military records of Bratunac to this day, especially since I worked at the then-secretariat for national defence. And as such, as a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as somebody fit for service in the army, I had to abide by the law on defence and law on the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I may stop you here. So if I understand your full and complete answer, at some point you did your military service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then after completing your military service, at some point you were asked to work for the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Because I served my military service in Knin, in Croatia, in the signal corps. I was a radio telegraph specialist. Back in 1980, personnel with those skills were needed in the defence department in Bratunac, representatives of the secretariat for defence had selected me out of several candidates, and I started working as a clerk for monitoring and reporting service for -- and for crypto protection. I continued in those tasks and duties until May of 1992, when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, today what is your position?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Starting in mid-May of 1992 and up until today, I've been working as chief of the defence department in Bratunac. The defence department is the smallest organisational unit of the defence department at the municipal level. This pertains to the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go step by step. So could you please just tell us just in general terms very briefly what exactly your department does.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the law on defence, the defence department deals with the following tasks: It keeps records of military conscripts, of materiel and technical equipment, and cattle as well as everything else that is needed for the defence of the country. In addition to that, the defence department deals with recruitment and sending of conscripts to perform or to serve their regular military service. Also, it deals with reinforcement and mobilisation of recruits, of conscripts, and materiel and technical equipment for wartime units, civilian defence units, for monitoring and reporting services, for communication units, and also coordinates that work with companies and enterprises when it comes to the obligation to perform labour. In addition to that, there's some general, administrative, and financial tasks that the department performs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to mobilisation, could you -- and briefly tell us exactly what do you mean when you say "mobilisation" and what exactly do you mobilise?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: When we use the term "mobilise," that means that at a particular point in time, upon an order from a superior organ, we are to call up either parts of units or an entire unit or carry out a general mobilisation, if that is what the order specifies. If it involves an exceptional situation, situation of imminent threat of war or war situation. Should I explain this in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask a couple of questions here. Now, how do you know which people to mobilise or what materiel you need to mobilise and where you would go to mobilise it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: All of those matters are specified in the plans that we maintain and that we have. Based on the needs of the army, the Main Staff creates certain plans for reinforcement of units, which are, following that, approved by the Ministry of Defence. Then this is sent to the defence department in order to be implemented or rather to carry out the reinforcement or the mobilisation, so that if there is an order to carry out a mobilisation, then the defence department will do so using a well-developed system. There is a general mobilisation and a partial one. Back when the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia existed, this system was quite well-developed, and that was the most important aspect of it. Once the mobilisation is carried out successfully, that signifies a top achievement for the Ministry of Defence. All of the preparations for defence would fail if the mobilisation were not carried out properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say that there was a system in place, could you tell us how the system was developed in case of need -- there was an emergency where you needed to mobilise, what sort of system existed and how was it possible for folks to engage in this mobilisation process.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Every conscript, even before that, was called up to the defence department, and his wartime deployment schedule was written down in his military booklet. So the call-up for mobilisation was performed on a form which had the title of MOB 11. That was the type of form, and there were two types of forms to be filled in. One was for general mobilisation and the other one was for partial mobilisation. And there was a well-organised courier system. We had couriers who would dispatch the invitations to attend, and all the conscripts were called up very quickly and mobilisation carried out in that way. This also referred to the mobilisation of materiel resources and technical resources, regardless of the fact whether they were privately owned or whether these resources before the war, as they were, they were socially owned. And as this -- there was state appropriation later on then. Usually these resources were in the hands of certain companies. When the mobilisation for materiel and technical resources was requested, the courier would take to the individual responsible in a given company, usually that was the managing director. He would be handed a call-up for mobilisation. He would take the piece of paper, the form, and sign for it, saying that he had received the call-up. And then he would be given a receipt for the resources that were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What if, Mr. Tesic, the need was of such an emergency that there was little time to contact everybody via courier? Was a process or method used to inform people that there was a mobilisation going on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Mobilisation can be proclaimed by the information media as well, that is to say it can be broadcast over the radio, it can be televised or posters can be put up in prominent places around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that all the men who were registered and had predetermined assignments in the event of mobilisation, was every male given a military assignment, or were there also nonmilitary assignments as part of this mobilisation process?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Let me explain that to you. The records for the military recruits is kept in the following manner: On one side we have these are assigned, and on the other side the nonassigned persons. And it -- not every conscript has to have a wartime assignment. It might be that there is no need at any given time for them to be assigned anywhere, although mostly all the human potential is kept in line with the strength of the units and their requirements and lists of their names are supplied to the various units and made up by the department itself. To make up the necessary number of men in the units, to have a full complement of soldiers, we need the department to look into this for civil defence purposes as well, the civil defence units and the working -- the enterprises and companies. They, too, are reinforced with military conscripts and those who were not. We can make up the numbers in that way, so the same applies to civilian protection or civil defence and in the monitoring and reporting service. But priority is always given to having the war units supplied with the necessary number of men, of soldiers, especially with young men, an officer's cadre, noncommissioned officers, on the basis of different specialty and training in the various army services and branches, if that is possible. And once that has been accomplished, then we use other people to make up the necessary numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated civil defence. Could you explain a little bit about what you mean by civil defence.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Civil defence or civilian protection is a separate segment of defence, and it is geared towards providing protection and safeguarding people, the inhabitants, and the society's material resources. Civil defence is organised in the following manner: There are staffs for civil defence and there are units for civil defence. The staffs, depending on the levels, whether there was a republican staff, for example, at the republican level and then lower down the regional staffs and the municipal staffs. In large enterprises, you could also have staffs at the level of the enterprise. So civil defence units, as a rule, were of general purpose. They were either of general purpose, that is to say, or specialised ones. The general purpose units were, for the most part, as far as we in Bratunac were concerned, were at the level of a platoon. And even before the war, every local community had one such unit. The special purpose ones were units for, for example, evacuation and safeguarding the population. Then there was another unit for blackouts. Then there was a unit for medical aid and assistance, first aid units that is, and first aid and veterinary assistance as well. There was also a unit for protecting and saving livestock and food of animal origin. Then there was a unit for transport and supplies and a unit for sanitation for the terrain and the biological and chemical protection unit. And I'm saying all this because we inherited this system from the old system that prevailed in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in which there was the generally known concept of Total National Defence, or all people's -- All People's Defence and Social Self Protection, in which everybody was incorporated into the system of defence; the citizen, as an individual, and society, as a whole. And nothing much changed later on, when the state of Yugoslavia actually disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you were in Bratunac and you were the head of this department for the Bratunac municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior -- how do you mean? At what point in time? Do you mean for a certain period of time? Because they changed. It wasn't the same one all the time. If you're thinking in 1995, for instance, then it was Stevan Ivanovic who was the secretary of the secretariat at the level of the region of Zvornik, if that's who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And based on this answer - and my question wasn't artfully put - I take it that Bratunac was part of a particular region?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Of course. I said previously that the Ministry of Defence is the executive organ set up by the government. And at the top is the Ministry of Defence, and then lower down the organisational units are the secretariats. And they are to be found in the regions. They have their headquarters in the individual regions; whereas the defence department was established as the lowest organisational unit of the Ministry of Defence in the local communities, so that the Bratunac local commune belonged to at that period of time the secretariat of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you -- if you recall, what other departments of municipalities belonged to the Zvornik secretariat or region?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that. Just let me think. Osmaci, Zvornik, Sekovici, Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, Skelani, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, and Srpsko Gorazde, as well as Srebrenica after the liberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Han Pijesak belonged to another secretariat, the Sarajevo secretariat, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How about Pale?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: And its headquarters was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Han Pijesak, and then I can give you the names of some other municipalities such as Sokolac and the surrounding municipalities like Rogatica and so on, I can't remember them all now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll discuss that later. Now, your department, who would you have direct contact with at your level?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: How do you mean contacts? You mean with the commands and units of the army or some other --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. With the commands and units of the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Mostly the departments would maintain contacts with the units or the commands of units with their area of responsibility in the municipality in which the department is located. So by the same token, since in Bratunac there was the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, I frequently contacted the command of the brigade. And most often I would contact and have dealings with Major Dragomir Eskic who was the head of the personnel department in the brigade. And very often during the war, I had contacts with the commanders of the brigade, because during the war there were very many of them in that brigade. And they -- one would replace the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, would a -- the corps, for instance, somebody from the Drina Corps, would they contact you if they needed your assistance for mobilisation of personnel or materiel within Bratunac? Would they come directly to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: From the corps you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Assuming the rules and the laws were followed.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Mostly, no. The corps is a superior command, so the corps would contact the secretariat. They were superior to me. And the secretariat was the higher instance, the higher organ, which was superior to me. So I would receive orders from the secretariat. They would be passed down to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the Main Staff? Could -- would the Main Staff, under the way the law is written, the way it's supposed to function, would the Main Staff come directly to you, or would they need to go to a higher echelon officer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be a precedent for the Main Staff to communicate lower down. The Main Staff contacted and had dealings with the Ministry of Defence at the highest level. So there was strict observance of the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we discuss the events of July 1995, I want to show you what has been marked as D60 -- or it has been introduced into evidence as D60. If you could please look at it. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what is this document, if you could just tell us very briefly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: This is the law on defence or the defence act, which was enacted by the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in June 1992. And it was in force and valid until a new law was passed, a new defence law and army act, in 1996 I believe. I'm not quite sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, does this law cover the various concepts that you spoke about with respect to mobilisation, civil defence, and what have you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. It regulates the work of the defence ministry, what kind of work it engages in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there are specific provisions. I don't want to go through provisions in order for the sake of saving some time, but in this law we would find provisions with respect to mobilisation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at article 10, for example, we will see that it says: "The Ministry of Defence shall carry out the mobilisation of the army, state organs, and organisations, civil defence units and staffs," et cetera, et cetera. And then that: "It shall keep records on personal and technical equipment for the purpose of conscription and mobilisation," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to slow down and I don't want -- there's no need to read out --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this law also provides for education with respect to civil defence, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the word "education," what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As far as drills and testing. So, for instance, if we were to go to article 64, 65, 68, we see that there are some specific provisions with respect to drills and training. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it that as part of -- let me ask you this: As part of your department, was it -- did you or did the Department of Defence conduct any drills or have any training in order to ensure that the mobilisation process of either people or materiel would work as it's supposed to work in time of an emergency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Attention was also paid to training for the courier system, because it was an all-important aspect of mobilisation. And if that was well-organised and if that functioned well, then mobilisation could be carried out very speedily and efficaciously in the time necessary. And special attention is paid to seeing that the units have the necessary number of soldiers, the priority units. There was classified A units, et cetera. So we want a full complement for units of that kind. And these -- the soldiers should be -- the conscripts should be nearby, able to report speedily, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And just -- again, I don't want to go through this because we can read it and analyse it at our leisure. But also we can find in here such as article 79 and 80 provisions that deal with punishment of punitive measures in the event citizens fail to respond to their duties and obligations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what is stated in article 79. If they fail to fulfill their materiel obligation, they will be punished. And if they are not prepared and trained for defence, if they do not perform their defence duties, if they do not perform their duties pursuant to civil defence. I don't know if you want me to explain all the different types of obligations and duties briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That won't be necessary at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But this law, would I be correct in concluding that this law more or less sets out the guidelines for your office, for your department and the Department of Defence, with respect to your tasks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. And of course the law can have bylaws and bills and provisions of various kinds to enhance it, and instructions and guidelines can be issued by the government or the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have no further questions on that. Now, if I can show you another document, what is marked as D114 for identification purposes. If you could please look at it. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: These are instructions from the Minister of Defence and this document was compiled on the 18th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there is another date I see on the front page which says 5 June 1995. Can you give us an explanation.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is the stamp when the document was received and when it arrived at the department. So from that day on is when I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Or rather, the defence department had received the document on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated you've seen this document. Do you have an original -- if I could speed it up a little bit. You provided us with a -- with the original of this document, have you not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And based on that, we copied that. And that's a copy of the original. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you have seen the original one here in The Hague since you've arrived. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I have it here for the record, in the event the Court or the Prosecution would like to have the original, which was -- this is a translation, incidentally, an official translation, by the registry. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, briefly if we could discuss this document, just very briefly. Could you tell us what these instructions set out to do.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: The minister says that the priority for reinforcing the ranks is for the army units, they must have a full complement. And then the other units and then that they be replenished. And then it regulates matters of how the units are to be replenished. That is to say that the corps commands should submit requests to the secretariat and then the secretariats send an order to the departments in the municipalities for certain units to be replenished. The Main Staff shall issue an order of its own expressly forbidding the commands of the army units to call-up and mobilise at their own initiative, or rather, to engage in the call-up of conscripts. And they are required to send in the request for replenishment to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could stop you here. So if I understand you correctly, the corps would make -- if the brigade needs something, they would ask the corps to make the request to the secretariat, and then the secretariat would pass down the order down to you. Is that how it would work?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we went down to paragraph number 5 on Exhibit D14 [sic] for identification purposes, do we see a deviation from what you just stated earlier?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we are dealing with exceptional circumstances, then the request to engage the reserve units may be sent by the command of the unit at the brigade level, directly to the defence department. However, providing that the corps command is immediately notified of that. This pertains to reserve units, to reserve units. I can clarify what reserve forces are. This involves a unit which is composed of military conscripts who had already had their assignments and enterprises, institutions, and companies pursuant to a labour obligation, not an obligation to serve in military service. However, I had an ability occasionally to use reserve forces if there is an urgent need to assist the military. Most often this involved 7- to 15-day assignments, following which they would go back to their companies to perform their labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in light of your explanation, is that the same as a Workers' Battalion, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I'm explaining. You've just used the term "Workers' Battalion." That's exactly what it is. This reserve forces from companies. They're called either Workers' Battalion or Work Battalion. That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I can show you what has been admitted into evidence -- admitted as P417A and this would be -- the B/C/S version is P417B. If I could show you this. Please look at it. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: This is the request, or rather, an order which came from the command of the Bratunac Brigade, pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the army, to carry out a full mobilisation of all military conscripts from the labour obligation until 1800 hours on the 10th of July. And on the second page, we have a table showing the engagement of military conscripts and their assignments in companies or enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: This is signed by -- this document is signed by somebody for the commander, and it was signed by Major Eskic, who was in charge of these personnel matters. This was quite frequent, that Major Eskic would sign such documents. I presume that he had been authorised to do so by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look up at the date, we can see what date this was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what is that date?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in looking at this document and looking at the instruction that we just discussed, would I be correct in concluding that this is -- this fits the exception that we read earlier, how the brigade commander could come directly to you, to your department, and make a request under extraordinary circumstances. Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That pertains to item 5, which regulates what exceptions they are in the instructions from the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And having looked at this document, do you recall whether this was executed, this was carried out, this order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I recall very well, because following the mobilisation of these persons, I personally took them to Pribicevac, this Workers' Battalion, and handed them over directly to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we going all the way to 3.30? I've kind of lost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- so I take it from that answer, on July 10th you recall being up in Pribicevac carrying out this task?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: To turn these people over with the list VOB 14, that's what the form is called, the form regulating how the people are transferred to a war unit, VOB 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the following day, just by way of reference, was the day that Srebrenica fell. Do you recall doing anything in particular on that day, having to carry out any particular orders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I returned from Pribicevac at 1.30 in the morning, so after midnight, with Major Eskic; we returned together. And I stayed at my office. On the 11th -- well, I can't remember exactly. I can't remember what I did on the 11th, but I was in my office mostly. We had other regular duties to discharge. I had to be always present in my office, because the army always needed something. And the army always turned to the Ministry of Defence when it needed something. So I couldn't be absent frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Do you know whether -- from your recollection whether you attended any meetings at the Hotel Fontana on that particular day, the day that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting at the Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether you were asked on that particular day now, we're talking about the 11th, the day that Srebrenica fell, whether you were called to attend any meetings that might have taken place at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I don't remember going to a meeting on the 11th. We had no time for meetings. On the 11th, there was combat going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the 12th, the day after Srebrenica has fallen, do you recall going to any meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us what was the first meeting that you attended.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me clarify how it was. The president of the Executive Board of Bratunac municipality Srbislav Davidovic, nicknamed Buco, asked me to take him in my private car to the command of the brigade, because his driver was not available. This was pursuant to an urgent notice to attend from General Mladic. And I did as I was asked. After -- or rather, it takes only 2 or 3 minutes to get by car from the municipal building to the command. As soon as I came back to the municipal building, as I was standing outside in front of the building, somebody told me - I don't know whether it was the secretary of the Executive Board or somebody else - somebody yelled to me through the window to go immediately to the command because I was also being asked to come by General Mladic. Again, I did as I was asked. I entered the operations room where the meeting was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you here. Where is the operations room?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: On the ground floor, to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The ground floor of the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade, which was located in the building of the Kaolin company. The company wasn't operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Blagojevic there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know who he was at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you saw him in the street, would you know this is Vidoje Blagojevic or would he just be some stranger to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I know Colonel Blagojevic very well. I've known him since he was appointed commander of the brigade, although I also remember him during the time when he was a student of the secondary school for construction in Bratunac. I think he's three or four years older than me. I think he was born in 1950, and he was the second year of students who started attending the school. Had he been there, I would have recognised him, certainly. But as I've said, I don't remember seeing him there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: -- in the operations room. Because there were some 10 to 15 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, before we discuss what happened at the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's okay, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, we left off on July 12th, 1995, when you were in the Bratunac Brigade operation room at a meeting that had been called by General Mladic. Now, could you please tell us, describe to us, to the best of your recollection what happened at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: At the meeting I stayed half an hour at the most. When I entered the operations room, I introduced myself as the head of the defence department, and I greeted General Mladic. He told me to sit down. Immediately after several introductory remarks concerning the event, the liberation of Srebrenica, he asked me directly: What do you think? What are we to do with all these people? I asked him: What people?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Did you know General Mladic before that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I used to see him because he would come to Bratunac. I don't remember whether it was just two times or more that he came to Bratunac before that. And once I saw him in Pale or rather at Jahorina and I think also in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he know you -- did he know exactly who you were if he were to see you on the street?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think he would recognise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So he asked you a question. And what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I asked him back: What people? And he said: The ones in Potocari. I didn't know about that. He said that there were a lot of Muslims up there and he had meant them. I thought for a little bit and then I said: Well, they should be sent to their territory, towards Kladanj and Tuzla. He didn't make any comment. And this is where it ended, as far as my conversation with Mladic is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for a bit longer in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you here. Now, do you recall, Mr. Tesic, being given any instructions or orders or requests from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I remember that he said that an urgent mobilisation or requisition of buses ought to be carried out as well as trailer trucks. In order to transport the population. Then he also said that transportation should be provided for at least 20.000 persons for that day or the following day at the latest. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was that an order to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic, as commander of the General Staff certainly wasn't joking when he said that. And a certain procedure was also observed as to how the orders are implemented in the written form. In view of the urgency, this order had to be dealt with immediately. And shortly thereafter a written order arrived from the secretariat in Zvornik to carry out a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you here. Now, when General Mladic gave you that information with respect to the people and the need for the buses, did he ask you to contact anyone in order for this mobilisation process to begin?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask anything in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you by any chance, based on that request, go to Colonel Blagojevic and ask him: Were there any orders for you to commence the mobilisation process, at least at the departmental level, at your level?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Tesic, get any requests from Colonel Blagojevic or anyone else that you recall from the Bratunac Brigade on his behalf to mobilise means of transportation available and registered in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that at one point in time, you received an order. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and that order came from where, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: It came from the secretariat in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before I show you some documents, Mr. Tesic, could you please inform us whether, based on General Mladic's comments to you about the need to mobilise buses and trucks for approximately 20.000 people, did you upon leaving the meeting place any phone calls to the secretariat or above the secretariat to the state level?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No. No. I did not contact anyone. I can say that we had just several buses in working order at the time. And I think that two or three buses had been requisitioned much earlier to the brigade in order to transport soldiers from time to time, from their homes back to the positions and so on. We had one bus which was intending to be used for the regular line between Bratunac and Belgrade, and that was a source of income for us. So we had nothing to requisition when it comes to buses. There was one privately owned bus owned by Radoljub Trisic. The bus was in a fairly poor condition, and I think that it was made operational at the workshop of the Vihor company. And then it was requisitioned. Now, as to the trailer trucks that at the meeting General Mladic requested as well, the only company that had those trailer trucks was the company called Vihor from Bratunac. However, trailer trucks were produced in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and there were frequent blockades on the border with Yugoslavia. And it was very difficult for trucks to go across the border. Therefore, in the territory of our municipality, in Bratunac, we had almost nothing we would requisition for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just one minor detail. When you did requisition a privately owned vehicle such as a bus, what was the procedure with respect to who would drive that particular bus that had been requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: In situations of that kind, it would be the owner of the motor vehicle who would usually be dissatisfied. He would complain because his wartime assignment was in the brigade and he didn't wish anybody else to drive his bus. So what he wanted to do was to drive it himself, to be able to take care of it, look after it better. And I think that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: So today, too, when they are distributed or when motor vehicles are used and other materiel and technical resources which are expensive, which are costly and when they are taken out from private owners, we always take care who we assign them to so that the principle should prevail according to which the driver is allowed to drive his own vehicle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The owner, interpreter's correction, the owner is allowed to drive his own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to show you a document that has been marked or has come in as an exhibit, P27 -- I'm sorry, 427. If you could look at this document. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- but I have shown you this document before coming into courtroom. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, having looked at it, could you please tell us a little bit about this document. What is it and ...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: This is a document which the command of the Drina Corps sent on the 12th of July, 1995, and it states urgent and relates to the provision of buses for the evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave. It is an order, ordered to the commands of the following brigades, including the Bratunac Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't have to -- okay very well. You don't have to read the whole document, just comment on it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: They are asking for all available buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: And it says that the corps command has already issued a request to the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska so that via the secretariat, the Ministry of Defence of Sarajevo and Zvornik, all available buses be mobilised or requisitioned from state and private persons and to be placed at the disposal -- placed at the disposal of people in Bratunac on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you here for a second. So if we go down to the third paragraph, we see that it's the corps that is making this request to the secretariat. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we have two secretariats, it would appear, Sarajevo and Zvornik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us from looking at this document what departments belonged to the Sarajevo secretariat.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo secretariat of the offices listed, what belongs to that is Sokolac, Rogatica, Han Pijesak, and the rest belonged to the Zvornik secretariat or command of the Zvornik secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So consistent with what you told us earlier that the corps would go to the secretariat, this would reflect this particular process. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me show you another document, what has -- which is Exhibit 434 -- P -- P434. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have I shown you this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And given your background, I take it you're comfortable commenting on this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please explain to us what conclusions you can draw from this particular document, P434.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: It can clearly be seen from this document that the command of the Drina Corps under very urgent addressed itself to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and pursuant to an order by the commander of the Main Staff with respect to providing 50 buses for evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave, they ask that diesel fuel be supplied as well as petrol for the buses. And we can see that it is a large-scale operation which surpasses the capabilities of the corps and its logistics, so that they are asking the Main Staff to help them out and to enable them to tank up on diesel fuel and petrol for the buses. And the signatory is the commander of the Drina Corps, Major General Milenko Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me show you another document, P426. I've shown you this document before, have I not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain to us how does this document perhaps relate to what we've already seen in the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document came from the defence ministry. It was sent from the defence ministry and addressed to the secretariat in Zvornik. And the subject is: Request for mobilisation or requisitioning of buses, on the basis of a request made by the Main Staff of the army. And the document is signed for the assistant minister, for those kinds of military affairs, Momcilo Kovacevic, but it was actually signed for him by Dragan Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, so, from this document it would appear, would it not, that it's the Main Staff making a direct request to the defence ministry. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. The hierarchy is being respected. How shall I put it? The horizontal and the vertical hierarchy down the line and across the board. Everybody knew who they were supposed to communicate with, at what level. The Main Staff with the Ministry of Defence and the corps with the secretariats and the units, or rather, the commands of the rank of brigade and regiment with the various departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, by -- if I could show you a couple of other documents as what has been marked for identification purposes as D118. For the record, this is from Mr. Butler's report, footnote 638. And I should say also for the record, the English version as an ERN 00889914. Sir, could you look at this document.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now could you tell us from this document, which is dated 13 July 1995, could you tell us what conclusions, if any, you can draw.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: The conclusions that I can draw are the following: Since the defence ministry sent out this request to the secretariat in Bijeljina - and this also refers to the requisitioning of buses - the conclusion I can make is this: That it is a broad-based operation which -- and that they need a great many buses. And that this surpasses the number of buses available in the Zvornik and Sarajevo region and that therefore the defence ministry issues orders to other secretariats, that is to say in this particular document to Bijeljina, the defence ministry of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me show you one other document, and that has been marked for identification purposes as D117. And it comes from, again, the Butler report, footnotes 241 and 638. And it has -- the English version has an ER number of 00960127. Could you please look at this document.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I've shown you this document as well, have I not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, from this document, what can you conclude, in light of your background and experience at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: This document once again is -- actually, from the heading we can't see that it is from the Ministry of Defence, but the signature is one that I can recognise. It is that of Dragan Kapetina signed for Momcilo Kovacevic. So I recognise his signature and this is a request for requisitioning or mobilisation addressed to the secretariat of Sarajevo, and they are asking for at least 20 buses from the municipalities of Pale, Sokolac, Rogatica, and Han Pijesak, that they, too, should report to Bratunac on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. One more document -- we actually have two more. This would be D120 for identification purposes and has an ER number of 03089736, a document obtained from the Office of the Prosecution. Could you look at that, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us if you can draw any conclusions from this particular document.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: From this document we can see that the secretariats - and in this specific case it is the secretariat of Zvornik - and they started to implement the order, to carry it out. In other words, this is an order to the departments or offices covered by the Zvornik secretariat, part of the department. That means Zvornik, Milici, Vlasenica, Sekovici, and Bratunac. So this is an order that was signed by Stephen Ivanovic, the secretary of the secretariat in Zvornik. And we can see that they are asking for the mobilisation of all buses except articulated ones. They are what we call the "harmonica" type of bus or "articulated bus". I think there was one such bus in Zvornik, and they were exempt from this requisitioning order. And that all regular lines should stop, should be cancelled, regular bus lines and services. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, this order, if I understand you correctly, would have come from the secretariat of your region to your department. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, correct me if I'm wrong, based on this order you would carry out the mobilisation process, which you eventually did. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could show you one other document, and this is D119 for identification purposes, with an ER number of 03089735.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: This seems to be the same thing, the Zvornik department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But could you -- it's slightly different than the previous one, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I notice the difference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But again, this is a request for mobilisation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, to the same municipalities from the secretariat of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, thank you -- I have no further questions with respect to the documents. Do you want to comment on these documents?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Just in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: This order includes the following: The mobilisation or requisitions of articulated trucks and buses, which means everything, all the vehicles are to be mobilised. The situation was so complex that there was great need for means of transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. Now, you indicated earlier that there was as far as mobilisation of transportation was concerned, there was very little available in Bratunac to be mobilised. Am I -- is that -- am I stating your testimony correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On July 12th, 1995, did you take any particular measures in seeking the mobilisation of what little resources were available in Bratunac, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether that was on the 12th, but it must have been. It probably was, because that was the order. I mean, the mobilisation of the bus we already mentioned from that private owner. His name was Radoljub Trisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But did you make any public announcements yourself in the Bratunac area, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No, because there was no need. We didn't have those capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to switch to, say, a larger area such as Zvornik where they would have, as I understand it, a fairly large public transportation or state-owned public transportation system. Am I correct in stating that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Zvornik they had a company for public transport. I think it was called Drinatrans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I'm using this just as an example. It doesn't have to be Zvornik; it could be anyplace else. Concretely, if you could tell us, how would the mobilisation process occur in order to mobilise all the available buses from that particular enterprise?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: That was very easily done. The Ministry of Defence had broad competencies and authorisation. And in its records, it already had a list of all the buses and trucks - and I've already said what records are kept by the defence department - which are registered. So in a very short space of time they can draw up lists of those vehicles. They take out their files, see what was recorded. They type out the list and refer to the order and issue their own order with a stamp and signature by the head of the department. They send the list to the company or anybody who has those vehicles, the vehicles they need. And pursuant to the law, they are duty-bound to hand over the vehicles to the spot designated and the vehicles must be in full working order. If we're dealing with a large municipality, then there's another possibility. A general mobilisation can be proclaimed and carried out of motor vehicles by putting up posters in public places, advertising this, and appealing to the population through the information media. Although I'm not well versed in that kind of thing because that's not what we did in my municipality and we didn't have anything to mobilise in actual fact. So I don't know whether my colleagues acted according to that procedure or not, but I assume they did in the other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just to make sure that we're all clear. With a transportation company it sounds as if with one courier they can mobilise the entire fleet of the transportation company?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes. If it's a higher interest that's at stake, the higher interests of defence or an extraordinary situation of any kind, that kind of thing, such as was the situation at that time, and it was covered by orders coming from the top levels of leadership, both as a request from the Main Staff of the army and also from the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, staying on July 12th, 1995, do you recall attending any other meetings on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where was the -- where did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: The meeting was at the SDS, in the offices there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And how was it that you got invited to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was a member of the municipal board of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us what you recall happened during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I think that it was sometime in the afternoon. I don't remember exactly what the time was. But I wasn't invited there -- or rather -- how shall I put this? It wasn't a party meeting in the strict sense of the word. Quite simply, all the -- all people in leadership positions in the municipality were there. And as Srebrenica had been freed, enormous problems resulted. And I myself in Potocari on that day, I stopped by for a short time and was able to see for myself the number of people that were in Potocari. So I assume that the president of the municipal board of the SDS of Bratunac - and his name was Miroslav Deronjic - as the number one man in Bratunac at that time, convened us all to tell us what the problems in hand were. And generally speaking, how we could get life back to normal in Srebrenica as soon as possible, because the situation up there was terrible. There was no water, there was no electricity. A lot of damage had been done, everything was very dirty. There were mounds of timber, of rubble, much more than at any other time. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: So in Srebrenica, the conditions were very bad. They were unhygienic conditions, and I myself personally saw this as soon as we approached Srebrenica. We began scratching ourselves. There were a lot of lice, fleas, and other such things, very ugly things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. During the meeting, sir - and I want to focus you on the meeting itself - was there any particular conversation that took place that you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I remember that at one point the secretary entered the room where the meeting was held and called Mr. Deronjic to the telephone. After quite a bit of time or after a little bit of time, Deronjic, with a smile on his face, told all of us that Mr. President, Radovan Karadzic, was on the line. And then he put it on the speakerphone so that all of us could hear the voice of the president. President Radovan Karadzic congratulated us on the liberation of Srebrenica and informed us that he had appointed Mr. Deronjic civilian commissioner for the municipality of Srebrenica, about which we were very happy. I don't know how to explain this, although Deronjic himself was probably a little bit concerned regarding this, because it was quite a challenge to organise a normal life in a town which had been isolated for two or more years. The enclave had lived under abnormal conditions for a long time. And then he said: Deronjic, I will hold you accountable for everything. Make sure that there is no looting there, that the companies are protected, and so on. This is what the conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he say anything about holding him accountable for the people?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying that. What he meant - at least that's what I thought - was the organisation of everyday life, cleaning of the city, organising new municipal government in Srebrenica. Because I think it was on the 12th that the state of war was declared in the Srebrenica area. I think that's when it was. Later on, he did become president of the War Presidency -- or no, I apologise. I can't remember. Maybe it wasn't that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Does the SDS office have a fax machine?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Later on, it did have. But back then I don't know. I know that they had a speakerphone. I assumed they did have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I apologise for not having the document here, but yesterday I did show you a document with respect to Mr. Deronjic's appointment, did I not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in reading the one paragraph, I believe it was paragraph number 5, 4 or 5, did you draw any conclusions as to what, based on that document, the president was imposing, what obligations and duties the president was imposing, on Mr. Deronjic as the commissioner for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I remember that yesterday when I looked at that document. That was the first time I saw it, therefore yesterday. I also remember that the date was the 11th. Now, as to when Deronjic received the fax, I don't know about that. If he received it on the 11th and called the meeting on the 12th, that would seem as though he invited us to celebrate his promotion and to hear the conversation with the president. As for your question about the specifics, I can't remember what the document said item by item. I would like to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So you don't recall whether the document imposed on Mr. Deronjic any particular duties with respect to the people from Potocari -- from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It appears now that counsel is leading the witness, and I don't think this is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, the witness told us that he did not see this document before, he just saw it yesterday. So I don't think your question will need --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was moving on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was Mr. Deronjic's response, Mr. Tesic? Did he say: Yes, Mr. President, I will take care of Srebrenica, don't worry? Did he say: I can't handle the situation? Did he make any comments?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. He didn't make any comments of that nature. He was happy. He might have said: Oh, this might be too much, as though he had taken up a lot upon his shoulders, a lot of duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there was an incident that occurred in Kravica, the Kravica warehouse. Did you hear about that incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see what had happened in Kravica, at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When did you see it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, just a bit before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. How is it, first of all, that you learned about the Kravica warehouse incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: I learned when I saw it, which is to say the defence department on the 14th of July had an obligation in view of the recruits who had been called up to serve their regular military service, and that was to send them to their military posts. Therefore, I organised bus transportation pursuant to order to the collection point or gathering point in Zvornik. This involved conscripts who were 18 and 19 years old, so young men who went to serve their regular military service. The road to Zvornik took them through Kravica, or rather, by the warehouse of Oka, which is a co-op in Kravica. This site was a painful one, and it surprised us. By the warehouse, almost its entire length, there were corpses lined up, the same way as one lines up logs. I don't know how many, perhaps even 2 or 300, but a lot. We couldn't drive fast because on the road we came across groups of soldiers, therefore we drove very slowly. It was painful for me, and I felt very uncomfortable in front of those children, because they are children after all. They were only 18 and 19, and I felt very uncomfortable that they had seen all that. Some -- after about half an hour from that warehouse in Oka, I arrived in Zvornik. I stayed there for 2 or 3 hours to hand over the recruits who were then sent further on to their military posts. After that, I returned back to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a couple of points. Were you sending those young boys, 18 and 19, to Zvornik because they had -- because of a special request, say, for instance to get involved in some sort of killing operation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No. No. I said that that was a regular planned sending of conscripts. These were young troops who went to serve their regular military service in their respective military posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Not to be confused with reservists?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR TESIC
utterances.text: These were young men who had not been trained up to then. They had just been recruited, and that was their first day of military service, which in those days lasted eight months I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it in light of your position, you would have something to do with civil protection, and in particular asanacija. Is that correct?
